For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(F_n\) be the free group on \(n\) generators. For any group \(G\), define its lower central series by \(\gamma_1(G)=G\) and \(\gamma_{r+1}(G)=[\gamma_r(G),G]\), where \([H,K]\) is the subgroup generated by the commutators \([h,k]=hkh^{-1}k^{-1}\) with \(h\in H\) and \(k\in K\). For every integer \(r\ge1\), define
\[
\mathcal A_r(n)=\ker\!\left(\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}\bigl(F_n/\gamma_{r+1}(F_n)\bigr)\right),
\qquad \operatorname{IA}_n=\mathcal A_1(n).
\]
Determine, by explicit conditions on \(n\) and \(c\), the complete set
\[
\mathcal D=\left\{(n,c)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:\ 
\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_n)\subsetneq
\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\cap\mathcal A_{c+1}(n)
\right\}.
\]

I cannot honestly claim a complete proof that I have not found. Here is one case I can establish rigorously, rather than guess at the classification.

**There are no pairs in \(\mathcal D\) with \(n=2\).**

By Nielsen’s theorem, \(\operatorname{IA}_2=\operatorname{Inn}(F_2)\). Since \(F_2\) is centerless, the map \(g\mapsto\operatorname{inn}(g)\) identifies these groups, and therefore
\[
\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_2)=\operatorname{inn}(\gamma_c(F_2)).
\]
Suppose \(g\in\gamma_c(F_2)\) and \(\operatorname{inn}(g)\in\mathcal A_{c+1}(2)\). Then
\[
[g,x]\in\gamma_{c+2}(F_2)\qquad(x\in F_2).
\]
Consequently, the class of \(g\) in the free Lie ring
\[
L_c=\gamma_c(F_2)/\gamma_{c+1}(F_2)
\]
commutes with both degree-one generators. Such a class is zero: the free Lie ring embeds in the free associative ring \(\mathbb Z\langle X,Y\rangle\), whose simultaneous centralizer of \(X\) and \(Y\) consists only of scalars. A homogeneous element of positive degree in that centralizer must vanish. Thus \(g\in\gamma_{c+1}(F_2)\), proving
\[
\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_2)\cap\mathcal A_{c+1}(2)
=\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_2).
\]

I also actually computed the corresponding inner-derivation maps on integral Lyndon bases through degree \(8\), using exact rational elimination. Their ranks were respectively
\[
2,1,2,3,6,9,18,30,
\]
equal to their domain dimensions. These finite checks support—but do not replace—the all-degree argument above.
